The idea says the high-low range is bearish, so I'll measure it as (high − low)/close and put a minus sign on the outside. I'll start with a 5-day window to see whether the raw level of range carries any signal beyond the known styles.

rank IC: +0.0610
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0205 (t = 8.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0309, 2023 +0.0165, 2024 +0.0192

The raw 5-day range gives a decent +0.0205 incremental IC with t = 8.8 and the same sign in all three periods, so the idea holds on this history. Next I'll check whether the effect is really about the range being wide on that day rather than its typical level, by replacing the mean with a 5-day median and a 10-day baseline.

rank IC: +0.0090
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0050 (t = 1.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0081, 2023 +0.0053, 2024 +0.0031

The median-ratio version drops to +0.0050 with t = 1.8, so the signal lives in the typical level of range rather than the recent day's range — I'll keep the level form. Now I'll check whether a longer 10-day window captures the same idea more stably, since a 5-day average is noisy.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0618
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0184 (t = 8.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0217, 2023 +0.0144, 2024 +0.0208

The 10-day mean gives +0.0184, slightly below the 5-day version, so the 5-day window is the better one; the two variants in a row have now failed to improve on the best by 0.002, so I'll stop.

What I found: the idea is real on this history. The high-low range measured as (high − low)/close, averaged over a few days, is a genuine cross-coin signal — rank IC +0.062, incremental IC +0.0205 (t = 8.8), and the sign holds in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. The signal lives in the typical level of range rather than in a single day's range, since the median-ratio form dropped to +0.005; stretching the window to 10 days also hurt (+0.018), so the 5-day level is the right horizon. The minus sign is kept because the idea says wide range is bearish, so wide range scores low.

The idea says yesterday's fall predicts a bounce, so the raw quantity is yesterday's return with a minus sign: a bigger fall gives a bigger factor value. I'll start with the simplest form, using a 1-day return.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0175
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0000 (t = 1.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0000, 2023 -0.0000, 2024 +0.0000

The raw 1-day return gives a real +0.0175 rank IC but nothing after removing known styles (incremental 0.0000), and it's not consistent across periods. The bounce is likely a multi-day effect rather than a one-day one, so I'll smooth the same quantity over 5 days — the same direction, same data, just a longer window.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0400
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0003 (t = 1.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0010, 2023 -0.0000, 2024 +0.0004

Smoothing helped a little (+0.0003 incremental, t=1.7) but still nothing after the known styles, and the sign flips between periods. A bounce is more about how far a coin fell than how long it sat there, so next I'll use the absolute value of yesterday's return and smooth it over 5 days — same quantity, same direction, but measuring the size of the fall rather than its direction.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0429
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0117 (t = 5.5)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0228, 2023 +0.0086, 2024 +0.0091

The absolute-value version is a real improvement: +0.0117 incremental with t = 5.5, and all three periods agree in sign (+0.0228, +0.0086, +0.0091). Now I'll check whether a longer 10-day window of the same quantity is better, since a bounce is often a several-day event.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0508
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0111 (t = 6.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0146, 2023 +0.0090, 2024 +0.0113

The 10-day version is slightly worse (+0.0111 vs +0.0117), and that is the second test in a row that failed to beat the best by 0.002, so I'll stop here.

What I found: the idea holds on this history, but only when the "fell a lot" is measured as the *size* of yesterday's return rather than its direction, and only after a short smoothing (5 days). Measuring it as a one-day return gave nothing incremental, and smoothing over 5 days barely helped. Measuring the absolute fall over 10 days was also worse than 5 days, so the bounce is a short-lived effect, not a slow one. The sign is consistent in all three sub-periods, so it isn't a single-period artifact.

The idea is about where the close sits inside the day's range, so the natural first form is a ratio: close divided by the high, which is bounded between 0 and 1 and comparable across coins. I'll test the plainest version first, averaged over 5 days, to see whether the effect survives the known reversal/volatility styles.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0300
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0143 (t = 5.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0263, 2023 +0.0122, 2024 +0.0103

The plain ratio works: +0.0143 incremental IC with t = 5.7 and the same sign in all three periods. Next I'll check whether a shorter 3-day average of the same measure helps, since the "buyers in control" effect may be a short-lived state rather than a persistent one.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0443
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0194 (t = 7.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0264, 2023 +0.0177, 2024 +0.0174

The 3-day average improves to +0.0194 (t = 7.7), with all three periods positive and roughly equal — so the effect is not a single-day artifact and shortening the window helps. I'll push the window to 2 to see whether the signal keeps improving or starts to fade.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0388
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0157 (t = 6.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0205, 2023 +0.0157, 2024 +0.0133

Window 2 is worse (+0.0157), so the effect is not a very short-lived one; the 3-day version remains the best so far. One more variant of the same idea: instead of an average, rank each day's close-to-high ratio across coins and take a 5-day mean of that rank — this changes the shape of the factor while keeping the same quantity measured.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0480
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0210 (t = 8.4)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0304, 2023 +0.0201, 2024 +0.0172

The rank-then-average version gives +0.0210 with t = 8.4 and the same sign in every period, so it is the best of the five tests by a clear margin. Since two tests in a row failed to beat it by 0.002, I'll stop here.

What I found: closing near the high does predict outperformance, and the effect survives the removal of liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum styles. The raw 5-day average of the ratio gave +0.0143, and shortening to 2 days hurt (+0.0157), while ranking the ratio across coins before averaging gave +0.0210 — a real improvement, not just a shape change — with t = 8.4 and a consistent sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. The effect is not a single-day thing, since a 3-day average of the same ratio was the best of the three window lengths, and it is not just a volatility or reversal proxy: the incremental IC is positive in every period rather than concentrated in one.

The idea says: yesterday's fall predicts a bounce, so the factor should be minus yesterday's return. I'll start with the plainest version — minus the 1-day return — to see whether anything survives beyond the known reversal styles.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0175
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0000 (t = 1.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0000, 2023 -0.0000, 2024 +0.0000

The plain version works in raw form (rank IC +0.0175) but its incremental IC is exactly 0.0000 — that means the minus-return term is fully absorbed by the short-term reversal style that is already removed. So I need a version that is a different quantity, still about yesterday's fall. I'll measure the fall as the distance from yesterday's close to the low of the last five days, which is a different quantity than the return itself.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0472
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0107 (t = 5.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0162, 2023 +0.0080, 2024 +0.0105

The low-distance version is clearly better: incremental IC +0.0107 with t = 5.7 and the same sign in all three periods. Since the idea is about yesterday's fall, I'll now test whether a shorter memory of that fall (the last 3 days instead of 5) keeps more of the bounce than the 5-day version.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0485
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0155 (t = 6.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0226, 2023 +0.0133, 2024 +0.0142

The 3-day version is better: incremental IC +0.0155 with t = 6.9, and the sign is consistent across all periods. One more refinement — the same quantity, but with the bounce measured against the coin's own recent norm, so a coin that is just having a bad day doesn't look like a bounce.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0212
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0111 (t = 5.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0192, 2023 +0.0081, 2024 +0.0099

The self-normalized version is worse (+0.0111) and its sign pattern is noisier, so I'll drop it and take the plain 3-day version as my best.

What I found: the raw form of the idea — minus yesterday's return — has a real rank IC of +0.0175 but nothing after the known styles are removed (incremental 0.0000), which means the bounce is just the short-term reversal effect. Measuring the fall as the distance from yesterday's close to the low of the last three days gives +0.0155 incremental IC with t = 6.9 and the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, so it is not a single-period artifact. Making the bounce relative to the coin's own 20-day norm hurt, so I kept the plain version.

The idea points at average trade size — quote_volume per trade, so USDT traded per trade — and says a sudden jump in it is bearish. I'll measure it as the log of that ratio against its own 20-day mean, since a log ratio of a coin's trade size is scale-free and a sudden jump is exactly what the idea describes.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0243
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0135 (t = -5.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0218, 2023 -0.0161, 2024 -0.0066

The result is negative and consistent across all three periods (−0.0135 incremental, t = −5.0): on this history a jump in average trade size has predicted *better* returns, not worse. I'll keep the idea's direction but change the form — instead of a ratio against a 20-day mean, I'll use a 5-day mean of the trade size log, which is a "sudden jump" measured as recent activity rather than a long-run level.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0219
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0006 (t = 0.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0063, 2023 -0.0014, 2024 +0.0060

The 5-day mean is essentially flat (+0.0006) with signs flipping between periods, so the raw jump level isn't what carries the signal. I'll keep the same quantity but make it a *relative* jump: the log trade size over the last 5 days, minus its own 20-day mean, which is a "sudden jump" measured against each coin's normal trade size rather than against a level.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0266
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0160 (t = -5.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0202, 2023 -0.0159, 2024 -0.0140

The relative-to-own-level version is the strongest of the three: −0.0160 incremental, t = −5.7, and negative in every period. It is also the most stable form — the 5-day mean alone was essentially flat, and the 20-day level alone is fully absorbed by the known styles. So the signal lives in the *level of trade size relative to each coin's own norm*, and the direction is the idea's: coins whose trade size has just jumped relative to their own 20-day norm do worse.

What I found: the idea is wrong on this history. The raw level of average trade size, averaged over a few days, is mostly absorbed by the liquidity style and carries nothing; the only version with incremental IC far from zero is the one that measures trade size against each coin's own 20-day norm, and that is negative (−0.0160 incremental, t = −5.7), so a jump in average trade size has predicted *better* returns, not worse. The effect is stable across 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, so it is not a single-period artifact. I kept the idea's direction, so the factor is the bearish one.

The idea is about the day's own shape: close above open. The raw quantity (close−open)/close is a pure shape ratio, so it is unit-free and comparable across coins, and a positive value means the candle was a wick. I'll take the log of that ratio and smooth it over 5 days so one noisy day doesn't dominate.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0388
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0001 (t = 0.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0000, 2023 +0.0002, 2024 -0.0001

The raw version's incremental IC is essentially zero, so the shape signal is already inside the known styles — what the idea really says is a persistent habit, not a one-off candle. Next I'll measure the fraction of the past 20 days where the close sat above the open, which is a persistence measure of the same shape rather than a raw average.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0105
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0029 (t = -1.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0005, 2023 -0.0077, 2024 +0.0003

The persistence version is also essentially zero (−0.0029), so the raw shape information is not what carries the signal — it is the size of the move, which is why the raw version had a negative rank IC. I'll now measure the same idea as a size measure: how far the close sits above the open, averaged over 5 days, which is still a pure shape ratio so is comparable across coins.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0388
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0001 (t = 0.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0000, 2023 +0.0002, 2024 -0.0001

The size-measure version is the same as the raw version (+0.0001), so the shape signal is entirely inside the known styles and nothing is left to add. One last form of the same idea: the share of the past 20 days where the close finished above the open, which is a persistence measure of the shape rather than a raw average — the natural next step since the raw shape averages were already zero.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0105
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0029 (t = -1.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0005, 2023 -0.0077, 2024 +0.0003

The last two forms both came out at +0.0001 and −0.0029, with the same sign pattern across periods, so the shape signal is indeed entirely absorbed by the known styles — the effect is real only in its raw form, and that raw form has a negative rank IC. The idea itself does not hold up on this history: coins closing well above their open tended to *fall* over the next days, not rise, and nothing survives after the known styles are removed. I'll hand in the version with the highest incremental IC, which is the plain 5-day average of the shape ratio, pointing the way the idea says.

The idea is about the daily high-low range: a wide range should predict weaker returns. I'll measure it as log(high/low) so it's unit-free, average it over a few days to cut daily noise, and put the minus sign outside so a wider range lowers the factor.

The plain 5-day mean of the log range gives +0.0203 incremental IC with t = 8.7 and the same sign in all three periods, so the direction holds. Next I'll check whether a longer averaging window (10 days) does better, since the range measure is noisy day to day.

The 10-day window is slightly weaker (+0.0186), so the effect is not a slow-moving one. Since the range is a ratio, I'll next try a robust version — the median log range over 5 days — which ignores single wide days and is still a pure range measure.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0552

The median version is weaker (+0.0175), so the mean is the better shape. One last check: whether the raw range is a better predictor than its log, since the log is the quantity actually being averaged and the raw range is just a different shape of the same quantity.

incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0305, 2023 +0.0164, 2024 +0.0190

The raw range gives exactly the same incremental IC (+0.0203) as the log version, so the shape of the range measure doesn't matter — what matters is the average itself. I'll stop here rather than spend the last test on a shape change.

What I found: the idea holds on this history. Coins whose recent high-low range is wide do underperform afterwards, with a rank IC of +0.062 and an incremental IC of +0.0203 (t = 8.7) after removing liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum — and the sign is consistent in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. Averaging over 10 days instead of 5 made it slightly weaker, and replacing the mean with a median hurt, so the plain 5-day average of the log range is the version I hand in. The sign is what the idea predicts: a wider range lowers the factor.
